strengths: Well-motivated problem: efficient surrogate modeling of ENVI-met microclimate simulations is genuinely useful for urban planning and public health applications.

The physics-informed graph representation is thoughtful: encoding shading, vegetation evapotranspiration, and wind-modulated convective diffusion as dynamically reconfigured edge types is a sensible way to inject temporal domain knowledge into graph learning, and it is clearly documented with parameter rationale (Appendix C).

A new benchmark dataset (UMC4/12) with 396 urban blocks, 2,500 nodes each, six target variables, and diverse urban morphologies stratified across Singapore is a valuable community resource if released as claimed.

The ablation and sensitivity studies are extensive: edge-type ablation, fusion strategies, prediction-head design, warming-up mechanism, feature ablation, k sensitivity, data-volume sensitivity, and computational profiling.
The paper is generally well written and organized, with clear problem formulation and honest acknowledgment of limitations (predefined physical priors may miss latent relationships).
weaknesses: Potential train/test leakage: the 1 km^2 simulation domains are partitioned into 250m blocks with a 50m overlap, so adjacent blocks share substantial spatial content. The paper never states whether the 70/20/10 split is by site, by block, or randomly, and random splitting over overlapping blocks would make the reported R^2 optimistic. This is a major evaluation validity concern.

All baselines are component-swapped variants of the authors' own architecture (same LSTM backbone, same encoders with RGCN swapped out). There are no established spatio-temporal GNN baselines (e.g., STGCN, DCRNN, AGCRN, T-GCN variants) or existing microclimate prediction methods (e.g., Kumar et al., KDD 2021), so the claimed state-of-the-art is not established against the field.

The headline improvements are overstated: 'up to 10.8% in R^2' is against the weakest baseline (CGAN); against the strongest baseline (GAE-LSTM, 0.8494) the R^2 gain is ~0.5% relative, and RMSE differences (~1.0535 vs 1.0682) are modest. Similarly, the 17.0% FLOPs reduction is only versus CGAN.

Internal inconsistencies raise reliability concerns: Table 2a reports Homo R^2 of 0.8336 while the text says 0.8347; Table A8 shows the Multi-Head variant achieving the same numbers as UrbanGraph in Table 1 with different FLOPs (9.21e9 vs 9.13e9), and the text says the main comparison uses a multi-head architecture while Appendix E shows single-head performs better — the configuration of the main model is confusing.

Generalization is very narrow: all data come from a single simulator (ENVI-met), a single city (Singapore), and a single extreme-heat day (08:00-19:00). There is no validation against real measurements and no cross-climate or cross-city transfer experiment, despite claims that the framework 'extends to broader urban heterogeneous dynamic computing tasks.'

The methodological novelty is incremental: the core model is RGCN + LSTM with hand-crafted rule-based edges, which the paper's own related work classifies as an existing 'observational bias' approach; the physics-informed dynamic edges are useful engineering rather than a new learning principle.

Some reported results are weak and unexplained: Table A12 shows R^2 of only 0.5159 (RH) and 0.5650 (AT) with very large variance (e.g., MRT ±0.2005), which undercuts the claimed strong generalization across target variables.
The reproducibility statement ends with 'publicly available at' followed by no URL; without a working code/dataset link, reproducibility cannot be verified.

Efficiency claims are partially undercut: UrbanGraph's inference speed (2.69 inf/s) is slower than RGCN-GRU (2.16) is not, but it is slower than GGAN-LSTM training per epoch comparisons show several baselines faster, and the FLOPs advantage over GCN/GINE baselines is minimal.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant problem (urban microclimate prediction) and the physics-informed heterogeneous/dynamic graph formulation is a reasonable and well-motivated framing: encoding shading, evapotranspiration, and wind-driven convection as typed, time-varying edges is intuitive and clearly described.

The released UMC4/12 dataset (ENVI-met simulations over 11 stratified Singapore sites, 396 blocks, six target variables, ~11.9M data points per variable) is a potentially useful community resource, and the dataset construction details (Appendix B) are documented reasonably thoroughly.

The ablation study is broad: heterogeneous vs. homogeneous graphs, dynamic vs. static topology, per-edge-type removal, input features, fusion strategies, prediction head design, k sensitivity, and training-data sensitivity are all covered.
Hyperparameters for all baselines are reported (Appendix D), and models are run over multiple independent trials with variance reported.
weaknesses: Severe mismatch between claims and evidence regarding generalization. The abstract claims the dataset covers 'diverse urban configurations and climates', but Appendix B reveals all data comes from a single extreme-heat day at Singapore Changi Airport EPW, in a single city and climate, over 08:00-19:00. No cross-city, cross-climate, or cross-season evaluation exists, so generalization claims (e.g., 'extends to broader urban heterogeneous dynamic computing tasks') are unsupported.

Evaluation is entirely on synthetic ENVI-met simulation data with no real-world validation (e.g., weather stations, mobile transects, sensor networks). The model is effectively a surrogate for one specific simulator; practical value is unclear, and simulator artifacts may be learned.

Baselines are weak and non-standard: they are constructed by swapping components of the authors' own architecture (GCN/GINE/RGCN variants, GAE, GGAN, CGAN, GRU/Transformer) rather than comparing against established spatio-temporal forecasting or physics-informed GNN methods cited in the related work (e.g., PIGNN-CFD, T-GCN-style models, or published microclimate predictors like Kumar et al. 2021). Using a CGAN and GAN-style models as regression baselines is questionable. The 'state-of-the-art' claim is therefore not credible.

The headline improvements are marginal and partially misleading. 'Improves R² by up to 10.8%' is measured against the weakest baseline (CGAN-LSTM); against the closest baseline (GAE-LSTM, 0.8494 vs. 0.8542) the gain is ~0.5%, comparable to the reported standard deviations, and no statistical significance testing is provided. The 17% FLOPs reduction is likewise against an outlier (RGCN-Transformer); UrbanGraph is not the fastest in training or inference in Table 1.

Potential data leakage: the 1 km² simulations are partitioned into 250m×250m blocks with 50m overlap, and the 70/20/10 split procedure is not specified as spatially or temporally disjoint. Overlapping blocks from the same simulation may appear in both train and test sets, inflating results.

Internal inconsistencies across experiments undermine confidence: the main comparison (Table 1) uses a multi-head prediction head with hidden dim 128, while ablations use an Optuna-tuned 384-dim, single-head model; Table A8 shows the single-head variant is actually better (0.8603 vs. 0.8542), yet Table 1 does not use it. Ablation 'Base' R² (0.8629) also does not match Table 1 (0.8542), making cross-table comparisons unreliable.
Multi-target 'generalization' results are weak: AT R² = 0.565 ± 0.132 and RH R² = 0.516 ± 0.204, which contradicts the claimed strong generalization; no baselines are reported for these targets.

The 'physics-informed' component is heuristic feature/edge engineering (hand-tuned clipping, fixed coefficients like λ_wind=0.3, R_base=5) rather than grounded physical modeling; the paper itself concedes (Appendix E.3/E.4) that explicit edge attributes/weights, the more physically principled design, did not help. The architectural novelty is limited to standard RGCN + LSTM composition.

The task setup is ambiguous about input availability: if future context vectors u_t (climate/time features) for the prediction window are assumed known at inference, the forecasting task is substantially easier and this should be stated; it is not clarified.

Presentation issues: the reproducbility statement is truncated with no URL ('publicly available at'); Figure 2 mislabels a static edge category as 'Relational graph convolutional networks'; a duplicated heading appears on page 6; typos such as 'framework,,' and an incomplete citation '(Heo et al.)' appear in the introduction.

Dataset scale is modest for a 'benchmark' claim: 11 sites from one city and one day, with blocks derived by windowing a small number of simulations, limits diversity and the benchmark's long-term value.

strengths: Novel and practically important problem formulation: urban microclimate field prediction is framed as dynamic heterogeneous graph learning, and the paper clearly articulates why physics-informed graph topology (shading, evapotranspiration, convective diffusion) differs from data-driven dynamic graphs in traffic-type tasks.

The physics-informed graph representation is well motivated and cleanly specified: five edge types (three dynamic, two static) with explicit construction rules (Eqs. 3-7) and documented parameter rationale in Appendix C.

The UMC4/12 dataset (11.9M data points per variable, 396 urban blocks, six target variables) is a genuine contribution as a first high-resolution benchmark for spatio-temporal microclimate modeling, with detailed documentation of generation, morphology stratification, and material assignments.

Unusually thorough ablation suite: heterogeneous/dynamic mechanisms, individual edge types, fusion strategies, prediction-head architectures, warming-up mechanism, edge attributes/weights, sensitivity to k and training volume, and computational scaling analysis.

Paper is generally well written and organized, with honest discussion of limitations (hand-designed topology may miss latent relationships) and a negative result (explicit edge weights/attributes did not help) reported transparently.
weaknesses: Headline claims are overstated relative to the evidence. The 'up to 10.8% R² improvement' is measured against the weakest baseline (CGAN-LSTM, 0.7712); against the strongest baseline (GAE-LSTM, 0.8494), the gain is ~1%, and the confidence intervals overlap (0.8542±.0044 vs 0.8494±.0036). No statistical significance tests are reported.

The efficiency claim is selectively framed. FLOPs reduction of 17% is only versus RGCN-Transformer (5.09e10); UrbanGraph (9.13e9) actually uses more FLOPs than RGCN-GRU (7.12e9) and GCN-LSTM (8.28e9), and its inference speed is not the best among baselines.

All baselines are internal component-swaps of the authors' own architecture (RGCN backbone + LSTM). No external state-of-the-art spatio-temporal or physics-informed GNN baselines (e.g., PIGNN-CFD, T-GCN-style models cited in related work, video/field prediction models) are compared, which weakens the 'state-of-the-art' claim.

Validation is entirely against ENVI-met simulations in a single city (Singapore) on a single extreme-heat-day type. The abstract claims the dataset covers 'diverse climates', which is not supported; there is no evaluation against real observational data, so the practical utility of the surrogate is unverified.
Generalization to other targets is weak: R² drops to 0.565 (AT) and 0.516 (RH) with large variance (±.13, ±.20), which undercuts the 'strong generalization capabilities' claim in the contributions.

Experimental setup inconsistencies: the main comparison uses hidden dim 128 with a multi-head architecture, while ablations/sensitivity use an Optuna-tuned hidden dim 384 with a single head, making ablation numbers (e.g., Base R²=0.8629) incomparable to Table 1 (0.8542). Table 2a text says R² drops to 0.8347 but the table reports 0.8336; Table 1 and Table A8 report different FLOPs (9.13e9 vs 9.21e9) for the same configuration. The 50m-overlapping block partitioning also raises concerns about spatial leakage between train/validation/test splits, but the split protocol is not clearly specified.
Several hand-tuned physical parameters (λwind=0.3, shadow angle 25°, Rbase=5) lack sensitivity analysis (only k is analyzed), and it is unclear whether these were tuned on validation or test data.
The reproducibility statement promises public code and dataset but contains no actual URL, and the paper ends mid-sentence, suggesting an incomplete submission.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: the paper targets a genuine gap in spatio-temporal urban microclimate prediction, where existing CNN/homogeneous GNN approaches fail to capture non-local, anisotropic, time-varying physical interactions.

The core idea—encoding time-varying physical first principles (shading geometry, wind-modulated advection, radiation-dependent vegetation activity) as hard structural constraints via dynamically reconfigured heterogeneous graph topology—is intuitive, physically grounded, and reasonably novel compared to soft-constraint (PINN) and data-driven dynamic graph approaches.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: broad baseline coverage across four categories (grid-based, static STGNN, generative graph, dynamic graph), extensive ablations (heterogeneity, dynamics, each edge type, fusion strategies, prediction heads, warming-up, edge features/weights, input features), sensitivity analyses (k, data volume), and computational profiling including a city-scale scalability stress test (~90k nodes).

Notable dataset and validation contributions: the UMC4/12 benchmark (11.9M data points, 396 blocks, 6 target variables, 4m/3m resolution) built from real geospatial data and ENVI-met simulations, with a two-tier validation strategy (micro-scale sensor calibration r > 0.73 and city-scale cross-validation against HiGTS with r = 0.842).

Generalization beyond the primary task: adaptation of the explicit topological encoding to a distinct physical domain (Navier-Stokes vector fields via UWF3D/OpenFOAM) with consistent gains over an isotropic Grid-GCN baseline supports the claimed generality of the paradigm.
Honest self-assessment: the Limitation section and Appendix E.3 (edge attributes/weights that did not help) demonstrate transparency rather than overclaiming.
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: the model is essentially an RGCN (off-the-shelf heterogeneous message passing) + LSTM with hand-crafted edge construction rules; the 'physical operator approximator' framing repackages standard RGCN relation-specific weights, and the 'causal pruning' terminology overstates what are heuristic threshold-based edge filters.

Marginal gains over the strongest baselines: UrbanGraph's R² = 0.8542 vs. RGCN-GRU 0.8483 and GAE-LSTM 0.8494 is a small improvement (~0.5–1.2 points), while the headline 73.8% FLOPs reduction is largely against the outlier LRGCN baseline (3.49e10 FLOPs), not the field at large.

Dataset generality concerns: the UMC4/12 benchmark derives from a single city (Singapore), a single extreme-heat day (08:00–19:00), and one simulator (ENVI-met); claims of a general 'first high-resolution benchmark' for microclimate modeling should be tempered by this narrow temporal, geographic, and physical coverage.

Hand-tuned physical parameters (R_base, λ_wind, shadow angle width, v_max) are justified heuristically and fixed a priori; the paper lacks an ablation over these thresholds, so the sensitivity of results to the 'physics' parameterization is unclear, and the 'derived from established urban physics literature' claim is not fully substantiated.

Internal inconsistencies weaken confidence: the main text states a multi-head prediction architecture while Appendix E shows the single-head variant performs better; ablations use a 384-dim Optuna-optimized model while main comparisons use 128-dim, making some cross-table comparisons (e.g., Base R² 0.8542 vs 0.8629) confusing; the baseline hyperparameter fairness rationale is asserted but only partially demonstrated.

Reproducibility gaps: the Reproducibility Statement contains no actual URL for code/data; several references are malformed (e.g., 'Xue; Qu et al., 2023', duplicated Li et al. 2019a/b entries, TLDR strings from Google Scholar); a text placeholder error appears in Appendix B.2.1 ('campus of the .') suggesting incomplete proofreading.

Efficiency claims could be better contextualized: FLOPs for dynamic graph models are not broken down by the cost of per-hour edge reconstruction, and inference speedups relative to baselines are modest (2.69 s/s vs. faster STGCN at 0.29 s/s).

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and under-explored problem (urban microclimate prediction) and proposes an intuitive physics-informed dynamic heterogeneous graph approach, encoding time-varying physical causality (shading, convection) as explicit graph structure.
A new high-resolution benchmark dataset (UMC4/12) is constructed from ENVI-met simulations over 396 urban blocks, potentially useful for the community.

The experimental section is extensive: comparisons against four categories of baselines, ablations on heterogeneity, dynamics, edge types, fusion, prediction heads, and sensitivity analyses, plus cross-domain evaluation on a Navier-Stokes wind-field dataset (UWF3D).
Real-world validation is attempted at two scales: sensor-based micro-scale calibration (r > 0.73) and city-scale comparison with the HiGTS dataset (r = 0.842).
The writing and figure quality are generally clear, and the method is well-motivated and easy to follow.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core model is a fairly standard RGCN + LSTM pipeline; the 'physics-informed' contribution amounts to hand-crafted heuristic edge-construction rules (Eqs. 3–7) with several manually tuned thresholds (shadow angle widths, base radii, wind coefficient, clipping bounds), which are more engineering heuristics than a principled or generalizable formalism. The claim of a 'generalizable explicit topological encoding paradigm' is stronger than the evidence.

Scope of evaluation is narrow: the main benchmark is derived from a single city (Singapore), a single extreme-heat day, and from ENVI-met — i.e., the model learns to imitate a simulator rather than real physics, which weakens the central claim of physical consistency and generalization. The city-scale validation uses coarse 0.1° reference data that can only support weak conclusions.

Efficiency claims are questionable: the 73.8% FLOPs reduction vs. LRGCN likely reflects architectural size differences rather than the benefit of 'explicit causal pruning'; moreover, training-time comparisons appear to exclude the per-timestep graph reconstruction cost, which for a 50k–90k node deployment is non-trivial. The claimed 'up to 10.8% improvement in R²' is against the weakest baseline; the gain over the strongest baseline (LRGCN) is only ~0.012 R².

Inconsistencies undermine rigor: the main results report R² = 0.8542 (hidden dim 128) while ablations use a different Optuna-tuned model (hidden dim 384, R² = 0.8629), making cross-comparisons confusing; there is an incomplete sentence ('deployed on the campus of the .'), a citation missing its year ('(Heo et al.)'), duplicated identical references (Li et al. 2019a/b), and a conspicuous blank URL in the reproducibility statement, so the promised public code/dataset cannot actually be verified.

Ablation gains are modest and the reported improvements (e.g., heterogeneous: +0.029 R²; dynamic: +0.057 R²) come from variants that also change other design choices, so attribution is not fully clean; significance testing across only 3 trials with ~10% test split from one day is limited.

Concerns about information leakage in evaluation: the global forcing vector includes ambient temperature, wind speed, and humidity, while the targets include AT, WS, and RH; although all baselines receive the same inputs, this setup reduces how impressive node-level prediction accuracy is.

Many design decisions (choice of LSTM over attention, static semantic edges, warming-up, k=8) appear empirically justified but add up to a system-level contribution whose components' individual novelty is low; the paper would benefit from sharper positioning of what is fundamentally new versus an application-tuned combination of known techniques.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly articulated problem: the paper identifies concrete limitations of homogeneous/static GNNs for urban microclimate prediction (uniform message passing, fixed topology) and proposes a coherent remedy — encoding time-varying physical causalities (shading, convection, evapotranspiration) directly into a dynamic heterogeneous graph topology as a hard structural inductive bias.

Comprehensive and well-designed evaluation: benchmarks against four categories of baselines (grid-based, static spatio-temporal GNNs, generative graph models, dynamic graph models), includes a controlled comparison of physics-injection strategies (none vs. soft PINN loss vs. hard structural constraint), and thorough ablations (heterogeneity, dynamic mechanism, edge types, fusion strategies, prediction heads, warming-up, edge features, multi-task vs. single-task).

Significant community contribution: the UMC4/12 benchmark — the first high-resolution spatio-temporal microclimate dataset (~11.9M data points per variable, 396 blocks, 6 target variables) — together with a two-tier real-world validation strategy (campus sensor network calibration, city-scale cross-validation against HiGTS) and a separate Navier-Stokes vector-field generalization study (UWF3D), substantially strengthens the empirical case.
Efficiency analysis is thoughtful: FLOPs, training time, inference speed, sensitivity to graph size, and a city-scale stress test (~90k nodes) demonstrating negligible edge-reconstruction cost.

The paper is generally well written, with clear problem formulation, explicit parameter rationales for heuristic thresholds, and honest acknowledgment of limitations (predefined physics may miss latent relationships; a Hybrid Topology direction is proposed).
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: the model is essentially a standard RGCN (Schlichtkrull et al., 2017) combined with an LSTM; the core contribution reduces to hand-crafted heuristic graph-construction rules (shadow geometry, wind-modulated distance, radii). The repeated use of 'causal pruning' is overclaimed — the rules are physical heuristics with tuned thresholds (λ_wind, Δφ_shadow, clip bounds), not verified causal structure.

Gains over the strongest baselines are modest and of unclear statistical significance: R² 0.8542 vs. GAE-LSTM 0.8494 and RGCN-GRU 0.8483 (differences within ~0.005–0.01, with reported standard deviations of similar magnitude). No significance tests are provided despite three runs. The efficiency story is also mixed: UrbanGraph trains slower than RGCN-GRU and STGCN and uses more FLOPs than STGCN, so 'state-of-the-art in both accuracy and efficiency' needs qualification.

FLOPs comparisons may be unfair or incomplete: the claimed 73.8% FLOPs reduction is measured only against LRGCN, and the cost of dynamic edge reconstruction per timestep is excluded from the FLOPs accounting.

Data diversity is limited: simulations cover a single extreme-heat day (08:00–19:00) in a single city (Singapore). Claims of generalization rest largely on ENVI-met self-consistency; the city-scale HiGTS validation uses 0.1°-resolution aggregated data, which is much coarser than the model's 4m resolution, so it mainly checks broad temporal trends rather than spatial fidelity.

Generalization on multiple targets is weaker than claimed: AT (R²=0.565) and RH (R²=0.516) perform considerably worse, yet the abstract/conclusion tout 'strong generalization capabilities' across target variables.

Confusing experimental setup: the main comparison uses hidden dim 128/multi-head while ablations use Optuna-optimized 384/single-head, so numbers are not directly comparable (Base R² 0.8629 vs. main result 0.8542); the claim that single-task learning is necessary is also in tension with the framing that 'we predict all six variables to demonstrate scalability.'

Reproducibility statement is incomplete (the release URL is blank in the manuscript), and there are notable editorial/citation problems (duplicated Li et al. 2019a/b entry, an incomplete reference 'Jiawei Xue...', a truncated sentence 'campus of the .', and a claim of a 3D grid while the method appears purely 2D without discussion of vertical processes).
